content: Leading player and sharer in the Lord Chamberlain's Men
Plays Berowne, Richard II, and Romeo
He answers a roar with a stuffed glove, and he does not get the page.
He looks at how a law-student king sits a hired horse, and he carries her sentence down to the inn.
He studies a borrowed majesty the way other men study a speech, from the knee and the elbow, and he comes away when the play is waiting.
He gave up the old lath sword at Holywell, said it had killed four Richmonds, and did not put it in the boy's hand.
He found the size of the part on the boards, and he would not wait on noon to know it.
He begins before the speech has landed, and then he waits so largely that the waiting commands the stage. The second time, the answer is smaller.
Rome sells, in his mouth, and he did not make you stay to admire it.
He was in the room, bored of a finished reckoning, and he did not decide.
He will leave his hand on the table for a line, and he will carry the leaves home without asking.
Given a glass to practise on, he looks a long moment, and it is not him who looks.
Offered a single Peace, he takes it, and he does not ask for a speech around it.
He offers to keep the sheets, and a refusal is a kind of care he will accept.
A month of learning has made him hungry for Verona, and he has worn a hole where the crown goes.
He plays a weak king as a strong man at being weak, and he will sit on the boards to do it.
When the afternoon has gone well he looks, and he says nothing, and the nothing is the praise.
He will take a clean figure and send it home, and he will not have it divided for the sake of the telling.
He will ask for a longer death down to the last night, and he will take the refusal and still go on and play.
He can hear the hall every night and still have nothing to add.
